cards.html:
Chapter 2: Git for CI/CD Work. CI/CD lives on top of Git. Every pipeline starts with a push, every review is a pull request, every rollback is a commit you can point to. You know commit, push, pull and branches; this chapter adds the tools that make you comfortable in a busy team repository.

After this level you can:

  • Work with feature branches, pull requests and a protected main.
  • Choose between merge and rebase, and clean up a PR with interactive rebase.
  • Resolve merge conflicts calmly, during a merge and during a rebase.
  • Park work with git stash; review a PR in parallel with git worktree.
  • Recover from mistakes with reflog, reset, revert, cherry-pick, and find a bad commit with bisect.

In a professional repository, nobody pushes directly to main. The branch is protected: changes arrive only through pull requests (PRs; GitLab calls them merge requests), which must pass CI and get a review before they can be merged. The basic loop (Figure 4):

  1. Update main and create a short-lived branch:

git switch -c feature/add-age-check.

  1. Make small, focused commits.
  2. Push the branch and open a PR. CI runs on the PR.
  3. Address review comments, keep the branch up to date with main.
  4. Merge. Delete the branch. main is deployable at all times.

Concept: Trunk-based development vs. GitFlow

Trunk-based development: everyone integrates into one branch (main, the "trunk") at least daily through small PRs; unfinished features hide behind feature flags. This is what CI was invented for and what most modern teams do. GitFlow uses long-lived develop, release/* and hotfix/* branches. It fits products with scheduled releases (e.g. installed software) but causes big, painful merges. For services and ML APIs, prefer trunk-based with short branches.
Your branch feature started from commit B. Meanwhile, teammates merged C and F into main. Before your PR can be merged, your branch must include their work. There are two ways to do that (Figure 5).

git merge main (while on feature) creates a new merge commit M with two parents. Nothing existing is changed. History is truthful but can get noisy: many "Merge branch main into feature" commits.

git rebase main takes your commits D and E, sets them aside, moves your branch to the tip of main, and replays them one by one as new commits D′ and E′. The result is a straight line, as if you had started your work today. But D′ and E′ have new commit IDs: history was rewritten.

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
Diagrams are one thing; here is what Git itself prints. In a test repository, feature has two commits and main gained two commits from a teammate in the meantime. git log --oneline --graph --all draws the history, newest first:

expected output:

* 9529ffb F: teammate feature
* 4d36953 C: teammate fix
| * 817122a E: test age check
| * 174de9c D: add age check
|/
* d4a7642 B: add loader
* 42c8734 A: initial

After git merge main on a copy of the branch, the graph has a diamond. D and E keep their IDs; a new merge commit 0e59e5a joins the two lines:

expected output:

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
*   0e59e5a Merge branch 'main' into feature-merge
|\
| * 9529ffb F: teammate feature
| * 4d36953 C: teammate fix
* | 817122a E: test age check
* | 174de9c D: add age check
|/
* d4a7642 B: add loader
* 42c8734 A: initial

After git rebase main on the original branch, the history is a straight line, and the IDs of D and E changed (174de9c → da2d582, 817122a → 89685ab), because each commit's ID is a hash of its content and its parent. New parent, new ID:

expected output:

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
* 89685ab E: test age check
* da2d582 D: add age check
* 9529ffb F: teammate feature
* 4d36953 C: teammate fix
* d4a7642 B: add loader
* 42c8734 A: initial

That last sentence is the key to everything that can go wrong with rebase: anybody who still has the old 174de9c now has a commit that no longer exists on your branch.

Try it: Make it a habit

Add an alias and look at the graph before and after every merge or rebase: git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all -20", then git lg. Most Git confusion disappears once you look at the graph instead of guessing.

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
Watch out: The golden rule of rebasing

Never rebase commits that other people have already based work on. Rebasing your own feature branch is fine, even after you pushed it (you then need git push --force-with-lease). Rebasing main or a branch a colleague also commits to will make their history diverge from yours.

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
SituationUseWhy
Update your feature branch with new maingit rebase main (or merge, if the team prefers)Clean, linear history; conflicts are solved commit by commit.
Branch is shared with a colleaguegit merge mainDoes not rewrite commits others have.
Integrating a finished PR into mainThe PR button: "Squash and merge" or "Rebase and merge"The team decides once, in the repository settings.
Pulling main when you have local commitsgit pull --rebaseAvoids pointless merge commits.

git pull is git fetch followed by git merge. With --rebase it is fetch + rebase instead. Make it the default once:

terminal:

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
git config --global pull.rebase true
git config --global rebase.autoStash true   # stash/unstash dirty files
git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3   # show the base, too

The usual way to update your branch before you ask for review:

terminal:

git switch feature/add-age-check
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main          # replay my commits on the newest main
uv run pytest                   # still green?
git push --force-with-lease     # update the PR (safe force push)

Concept: Why --force-with-lease, never --force

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
After a rebase, your local branch and the remote branch have different histories, so a normal push is rejected. --force would overwrite the remote unconditionally, including commits a colleague pushed in the meantime. --force-with-lease only overwrites if the remote is still where you last saw it; otherwise it refuses.

This is what a normal push looks like after a rebase, and what the lease does when a colleague pushed to the same branch meanwhile (real output, remote URL shortened):

expected output:

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
$ git push
 ! [rejected]        feature/x -> feature/x (fetch first)
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. ...

$ git push --force-with-lease
 ! [rejected]        feature/x -> feature/x (stale info)

"Stale info" means: the remote branch is no longer where your last fetch saw it, so somebody else pushed. Stop and look before you do anything else.

What if… I run git fetch and then --force-with-lease again?

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
What happens: The push succeeds, and your colleague's commit is gone from the remote branch:

$ git fetch
$ git push --force-with-lease
 + e00e90c...4081a71 feature/x -> feature/x (forced update)

It gets worse. When the colleague runs git pull --rebase, Git sees that their commit used to be on origin/feature/x and assumes it was intentionally removed upstream, so it silently drops it from their branch too. We ran exactly this; the colleague's log afterwards no longer contains "feat: colleague adds part 2".

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
Why: The lease compares against your remote-tracking branch (origin/feature/x). git fetch updates that to the colleague's commit, so the lease now "expects" it and lets you overwrite it. You never looked at what you fetched.

What you do: Prevent it with git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes (Git 2.30+). It also checks that the remote tip is part of your local history, and it rejected our push with (remote ref updated since checkout). Make it the default: git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true. Before any force push, run git log --oneline HEAD..origin/feature/x: if it prints anything, those commits exist only remotely; integrate them first (git rebase origin/feature/x). To rescue a lost commit: the colleague finds it in git reflog (it was HEAD@{2} in our run) and runs git cherry-pick <sha>.

cards.sub: Worked example: the same branch, merged and rebased
cards.html:
What if… a colleague rebased a branch I also work on?

What happens: Your git pull stops with fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches, or a plain merge produces every commit twice (old ID and new ID side by side).

Why: Your local branch has the old commits, the remote has the rewritten ones. Git sees two different histories.

What you do: If you have no local work of your own: git fetch then git reset --hard origin/<branch> (look at git status first: this discards uncommitted changes). If you have local commits: git pull --rebase, which skips commits that are already upstream in rewritten form and replays only yours. Then agree with the team: shared branches are merged, never rebased.

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.html:
Your PR has six commits: "add age check", "fix typo", "wip", "add test for age", "oops forgot file", "fix lint". Reviewers want two meaningful commits. Interactive rebase lets you edit the list of commits like a text file:

terminal:

git rebase -i origin/main      # all commits not yet on main
# or: git rebase -i HEAD~6       # the last six commits

Git opens your editor with a todo list, oldest commit first:

git-rebase-todo:

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.html:
pick 3f2a1c0 add age check
pick 9b81d44 fix typo
pick 0c7e5aa wip
pick 51d2f9b add test for age
pick a77e0b3 oops forgot file
pick e41c2d8 fix lint

# Commands:
# p, pick = use commit           r, reword = use commit, edit message
# e, edit = stop to amend it     s, squash = meld into previous, keep msg
# f, fixup = meld into previous, discard this message
# d, drop = remove commit        (reorder lines to reorder commits)

Change the words and the order, save and close:

git-rebase-todo (edited):

reword 3f2a1c0 add age check
fixup 9b81d44 fix typo
fixup 0c7e5aa wip
fixup e41c2d8 fix lint
pick 51d2f9b add test for age
fixup a77e0b3 oops forgot file

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.html:
Git replays the commits; reword opens the editor once more so you can write feat: add age check. The result is shown in Figure 6.

Try it: Let Git prepare the todo list

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.html: If you know while working that a commit fixes an earlier one, commit it with git commit --fixup 3f2a1c0. Later, git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main puts every fixup line in the right place automatically.

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.sub: Worked example: split one commit into two
cards.html:
Reviewers ask you to separate "refactor the loader" from "add age validation", but both are in one commit 51d2f9b. The edit command stops the rebase at that commit so you can rebuild it:

terminal:

git rebase -i origin/main     # change 'pick 51d2f9b' to 'edit 51d2f9b'
# Git stops: 'Stopped at 51d2f9b... add age check and refactor loader'
git reset HEAD~1              # undo the commit, keep its changes unstaged
git add src/credit_api/data.py
git commit -m "refactor: simplify loader"
git add src/credit_api/validation.py tests/test_data.py
git commit -m "feat: reject applicants under 18"
git rebase --continue         # replay the remaining commits

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.sub: Worked example: split one commit into two
cards.html:
git add -p (patch mode) goes one step further: it shows each changed hunk and asks Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,s,e,?]?, so you can split changes inside one file into separate commits. It is the single most useful command for making reviewable commits.

What if… the interactive rebase went wrong and I already finished it?

What happens: You dropped the wrong line in the todo list, or squashed into the wrong commit. The rebase finished; the branch looks wrong.

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.sub: Worked example: split one commit into two
cards.html:
What you do: Before the rebase started, Git saved the old tip in ORIG_HEAD. Right after the rebase, git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD restores the branch exactly. If you ran other commands since (which overwrite ORIG_HEAD), use git reflog and look for the line before rebase (start), then git reset --hard HEAD@{n}. While a rebase is still in progress, git rebase --abort is simpler.

What if… my PR is based on a colleague's PR that was squash-merged?

What happens: You built feat/b on top of feat/a ("stacked PRs"). feat/a was squash-merged into main as one new commit S. Now git rebase main on feat/b tries to replay feat/a's original commits again and conflicts with S everywhere.

cards.s: Interactive rebase: clean up before review
cards.sub: Worked example: split one commit into two
cards.html:
Why: A squash creates a new commit with new content; Git cannot tell that feat/a's commits are already in main.

What you do: Transplant only your commits: git rebase --onto main feat/a feat/b means "take the commits of feat/b that are not in feat/a and replay them onto main". (If feat/a was already deleted, use the SHA of its last commit instead of the name; git log on your branch still shows it.)

cards.s: Commit messages that machines can read
cards.html:
Conventional Commits is a simple format for commit messages: type(scope): description, e.g. feat(api): add /version endpoint or fix: handle unknown purpose category.

TypeUse forVersion bump
featA new feature for users of the API or model.minor: 1.4.0 → 1.5.0
fixA bug fix.patch: 1.4.0 → 1.4.1
feat! or BREAKING CHANGE: footerA change that breaks clients.major: 1.4.0 → 2.0.0
docs, test, refactor, ci, chore, perfEverything else.none

cards.s: Commit messages that machines can read
cards.html:
Because the type is machine-readable, CI can generate changelogs and release versions automatically (tools: release-please, semantic-release; commitlint checks the format in CI). With squash merges, the PR title becomes the commit message, so teams often lint PR titles instead.

Exercise: Rebase with conflicts

In the conflict lab, add two more commits on feature/stricter that each change features: to a different value, and one commit on main that changes features: too. Rebase the feature branch onto main. How many times do you have to resolve? Then use git reflog to get back to the state before the rebase.

Exercise: Clean history

cards.s: Commit messages that machines can read
cards.html:
Create five small commits on a branch, including two "fix typo" commits. Use git commit --fixup for one of them and git rebase -i --autosquash to end up with two Conventional-Commit messages.

Exercise: The force-push trap

Create a bare repository (git init --bare remote.git) and two clones, you and colleague. Reproduce the what-if from Section 2.2: both push to feature/x, you rebase, fetch, and force-push with the lease. Confirm the colleague's commit disappears, recover it from the colleague's reflog, then repeat with --force-if-includes and observe the rejection.

Exercise: Lock file conflict

In a fresh uv init project, add a different dependency on two branches and merge them. Resolve it the right way, and prove it with uv sync --locked.

cards.s: Commit messages that machines can read
cards.html:
Exercise: Semantic conflict

Reproduce the "no conflict, still broken" what-if with two branches and a test. Which GitHub setting would have prevented the broken main, and at what cost?

Checkpoint: you should now be able to…

  • explain merge vs. rebase with a drawing, and state the golden rule;
  • update a feature branch with git rebase origin/main and push with

--force-with-lease;

cards.s: Commit messages that machines can read
cards.html:
• squash, reword, reorder and drop commits with git rebase -i;
  • read conflict markers, resolve them in VS Code or the terminal, and use --abort / --continue;
  • read the base section of a zdiff3 conflict and resolve by intention; handle modify/delete, lock-file and binary conflicts;
  • explain why --force-if-includes exists, why a reverted merge must be reverted again before re-merging, and what a semantic conflict is;
  • choose between stash and worktree;
  • undo with reset, revert and reflog, and find a bad commit with git bisect run.
